summary: Ethernet VPN offers multihoming VPN service across MPLS/IP for connectivity inside a subnet. This document describes an Integrated Routing and Bridging solution built on EVPN for efficient inter-subnet connectivity between tenant systems while keeping EVPN's multihoming capabilities.

plainLanguage.summary:
EVPN connects hosts that share a subnet. RFC 9135 lets each provider edge router also route between subnets, so traffic between two subnets goes directly between the routers instead of being sent to a central gateway and back.

It defines two ways to do this. Symmetric mode scales better but needs more work at each end; asymmetric mode keeps the control plane simpler but makes the first router keep a record of every remote host.

questions: what is an irb interface in evpn
subtitle: How EVPN edge routers can both bridge and route tenant traffic locally, without sending it to a central gateway and back.

tldr.problem: EVPN connects hosts inside one subnet, but traffic between subnets had to be sent to a centralized Layer 3 gateway and back, which is inefficient and sometimes impractical in large multi-tenant data centers.
tldr.mechanism: Each provider edge router gets Integrated Routing and Bridging (IRB): it bridges within a subnet and routes between subnets packet by packet. The RFC defines two modes, symmetric and asymmetric, plus the BGP routes and host-mobility procedures that support them.
tldr.outcome: Inter-subnet traffic is routed at the edge while EVPN's multihoming is kept. Symmetric IRB scales better, asymmetric IRB keeps the control plane simpler, and the operator chooses.

today: RFC 9135 was published in October 2021 and is a Proposed Standard. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Routing Moves to the Edge
sections.content:
EVPN, described in RFC 7432, gives a multihoming VPN service over an MPLS or IP network for hosts inside one subnet. An IP subnet is represented by an EVPN instance, or by an EVPN instance together with a VLAN for a VLAN-aware bundle service.

Traffic between two subnets normally goes to a central Layer 3 gateway. When two hosts in different subnets attached to the same provider edge router needed to talk, their traffic was sent from that router all the way to the central gateway and back again. In a large multi-tenant data centre that is inefficient and sometimes impractical.

This document specifies Integrated Routing and Bridging (IRB) on the provider edge routers. A router with IRB bridges traffic inside a subnet and routes traffic between subnets packet by packet, so the traffic never leaves the edge. The RFC states two requirements: a tenant's inter-subnet IP traffic is routed and its intra-subnet and non-routable traffic is bridged, and IP routing of inter-subnet traffic can be switched off per VLAN on routers that backhaul that traffic to another router for routing.
sections.plainLanguage: EVPN connects hosts that share a subnet. Traffic between different subnets used to be sent to a central gateway and back, which wastes bandwidth in a large data centre. This document lets each edge router do the routing itself, so the traffic goes straight between the routers that need it.

sections.title: The PE Model: MAC-VRFs, IP-VRFs and IRB Interfaces
sections.content:
A tenant on a provider edge router has an IP-VRF, the IP routing table for that tenant, and one or more MAC-VRFs, the Layer 2 tables for that tenant. A MAC-VRF contains one bridge table per VLAN, and each bridge table is one broadcast domain, which this document treats as equivalent to a subnet.

Each bridge table is joined to the IP-VRF by a Layer 3 interface called an IRB interface. Since one subnet is normally one VLAN and so one bridge table, a tenant with several subnets has several IRB interfaces. The IRB interface carries the default gateway IP and MAC addresses that the tenant's hosts use.

Both the IP-VRF and the MAC-VRF are identified by a Route Target and a Route Distinguisher. In the VLAN-based mode of RFC 7432 there is one bridge table per MAC-VRF, so the Route Target alone identifies it. In the VLAN-aware bundle mode there are several bridge tables per MAC-VRF, so the receiving router needs both the Route Target and the VLAN ID.
sections.plainLanguage: Each tenant has an IP routing table and one or more Layer 2 tables, one per VLAN. A Layer 3 interface joins each VLAN's table to the routing table, and that interface holds the default gateway address the tenant's hosts send their traffic to.

sections.title: Symmetric and Asymmetric IRB
sections.content:
The RFC defines two ways to forward traffic between subnets, and the choice belongs to the operator.

In symmetric IRB, both ends do the same amount of work. The ingress router looks up the destination MAC address, then looks up the destination IP address, and forwards between the two tenants' IP-VRFs. The egress router looks up the IP address and then the MAC address. Because the tunnel connects IP-VRFs, it can be an IP-only tunnel or an Ethernet tunnel. Each router keeps ARP entries only for hosts connected to it.

In asymmetric IRB, the ingress router does three lookups and the egress router does one. The forwarding is between the tenants' MAC-VRFs, so the tunnel must be an Ethernet tunnel, and the packet must carry the destination host's MAC address. The ingress router therefore keeps an ARP entry for every remote host, and keeps a bridge table and an IRB interface for every subnet in the tenant's IP-VRF, including subnets with no local hosts. That is why the RFC says the scale of the ARP table, the IRB interfaces and the bridge tables needs careful thought before choosing this mode.

One further difference shows up in the TTL. Whenever a router performs a host IP lookup for a routed packet, the TTL or hop limit is decremented by one and the packet is dropped if it reaches zero. Symmetric IRB decrements it at both the ingress and the egress router; asymmetric IRB decrements it only at the ingress router.
sections.plainLanguage: In symmetric mode both routers look up the address and then the hardware address. In asymmetric mode the first router does all of that and the second router does a single hardware lookup, which means the first router has to keep a record of every remote host. Symmetric mode scales better; asymmetric mode keeps the control plane simpler.

sections.title: The Gateway Addresses of an IRB Interface
sections.content:
The router acts as the default gateway for the tenant's hosts, and the RFC gives two ways to configure the gateway addresses on an IRB interface.

  • All the routers for a tenant subnet use the same anycast gateway IP address and the same anycast gateway MAC address.
  • All the routers for a tenant subnet use the same anycast gateway IP address, but each router uses its own MAC address. These are tied to the shared IP address with the Default Gateway extended community of RFC 7432, carried in the EVPN MAC/IP Advertisement routes.

The RFC recommends the first option, because it is simpler to provision and needs no extended community or MAC aliasing, and because after a host moves it does not have to refresh its gateway entry. It also matters when the tenant's applications check MAC addresses: with an anycast MAC the traffic always comes from the same address the host sends to. With the second option, the IRB interface MAC address MUST be the one used in the initial ARP reply or Neighbor Advertisement for that host.

An implementation MAY derive the anycast MAC automatically, from the ranges defined in RFC 5798: 00-00-5E-00-01-{VRID} for IPv4 and 00-00-5E-00-02-{VRID} for IPv6. The last octet comes from a configurable Virtual Router ID in the range 1 to 255, defaulting to 1. Automatic derivation may only be used when there is certainty that the derived MAC does not collide with a customer MAC address.
sections.plainLanguage: The router presents itself to the tenant's hosts as the default gateway. The recommended setup gives every router for a subnet the same gateway IP and the same hardware address, so a host that moves does not have to refresh anything.

sections.title: Routes and Forwarding in Symmetric IRB
sections.content:
When a router learns a host's MAC and IP address, it installs them in the tenant's bridge table, in the IP-VRF and in its ARP table or Neighbor Discovery cache, and then advertises an EVPN MAC/IP Advertisement route, route type 2, to the other routers in the tenant's VPN. The Length field of that route MUST be 40 when it carries an IPv4 address and 52 when it carries an IPv6 address. The second MPLS label field holds the label or VNI of the tenant's IP-VRF. The route is advertised with two Route Targets, one for the MAC-VRF and one for the IP-VRF, and with an EVPN Router's MAC extended community that carries the advertising router's MAC address. The advertising router SHALL attach only one such extended community to a route.

On receipt, the receiving router uses the MAC-VRF Route Target and the Ethernet Tag to find the bridge table and imports the MAC address, and uses the IP-VRF Route Target to find the routing table and imports the IP address. If the second label field is non-zero, the route is to be used for symmetric IRB, and the label value is used when sending a packet for that IP address to the advertising router. A router that supports only asymmetric IRB MUST ignore the second label field and install the MAC address and the IP-to-MAC association instead.

A router that has hosts in a subnet must advertise that subnet as an EVPN route type 5, so that a router elsewhere can send a packet to the right place when it does not yet know the host's address. Once the packet arrives, the receiving router floods an ARP request across the Layer 2 overlay, the host answers, and the address is learned and advertised. Later packets go straight to the host.
sections.plainLanguage: When a router learns a host's addresses, it tells the other routers about them in a BGP route that carries the hardware address, the IP address and a label for the tenant's routing table. The other routers import what they need from it. If a router has never heard of a host, it first learns the subnet route so it knows where to send the packet, and the router on the far side then asks the host directly.

sections.title: Host Mobility
sections.content:
The RFC describes three cases when a host moves from one router to another.

  • The host sends a gratuitous ARP on arrival. The new router updates its tables, sees that it already knew the address from the old router, and starts the MAC mobility procedure from RFC 7432: it advertises the route again with the MAC Mobility extended community and the sequence number increased by one. The old router updates its tables to point at the new router, withdraws its own route, and sends an ARP probe to check that the host really has gone; if the host answers, it re-advertises with a higher sequence number. Every other router compares sequence numbers and updates only when the new one is higher.
  • The host sends data without an ARP request. The new router learns the MAC address from the data plane and starts the same mobility procedure. The old router sends an ARP probe for the IP and MAC pair, both locally and to the other routers in the subnet.
  • The host is silent and sends nothing at all. Neither router notices. An age-out timer on the old router triggers the ARP probe, which then works as in the previous case.

In symmetric IRB the old router removes the entry for the moved address from its local ARP table; in asymmetric IRB it updates that entry with the new adjacency. The procedures assume a one-to-one relationship between a host's MAC address and its IP address.
sections.plainLanguage: When a host moves to another router, the new router notices it already knew that address and tells everyone else, with a number that goes up each time. Routers update their tables only when the number is higher than what they have. If the host says nothing at all, a timer on the old router eventually sends a probe to find out.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The Layer 2 security considerations follow those of RFC 7432 for MPLS and of RFC 8365 for VXLAN or NVGRE. The Layer 3 considerations follow RFC 4365, except that the customer devices here do not run dynamic routing protocols. The RFC treats that as a security advantage, because dynamic routing protocols can be blocked on the attachment circuits so that a tenant cannot interact with the provider's own routing protocols.

The VPN scheme described here does not provide the four properties listed in RFC 4365: confidentiality, source authentication, integrity protection and replay protection. If they are wanted, they have to come from mechanisms outside the VPN.

One detail is worth noting. Where the EVPN route type 5 is used, it carries an Overlay Index that has to be resolved through another EVPN route, the route type 2. Any filtering or modification of that route type 2 changes the resolution of the route type 5 and therefore changes where the packets go.
sections.plainLanguage: The scheme does not encrypt tenant traffic or prove who sent it; those have to come from somewhere else. One thing to watch is that the route used to carry a subnet prefix depends on another route, so changing that second route changes where the traffic goes.
